question: What did you like most about this prompt?
answer: The clear split between what is fixed and what is open. The engine, the hub protocol, 10% music and the controller-first rules are nailed down, while genre, camera, story and scope are mine to decide. The 'This computer' section was the most useful part: exact tool versions and named stand-ins for missing hardware meant I could test the risky parts of the plan here instead of guessing, and that found real problems before any builder hits them.

question: What was confusing?
answer: Five things. (1) 'Follow the hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': the hub README covers sessions and says the game simply runs as usual outside one, so it does not say what multiplayer on its own should be. I decided on couch co-op on one screen. (2) 'Capture what makes the source distinctive (its world, characters, themes and tone)' pulls against 'build an original game'. I kept the themes, tone and mechanics and made the world and characters new. (3) 'Prefer file://' meets the engine guide's 'ES modules don't load from file://'. It only resolves once everything is bundled inline, which I tested. (4) The WebGPU flags in the notes lose the GPU device with this engine within seconds. The kit's check.mjs has a longer list that works. (5) TASK.md is written to the builder, so as the planner I had to work out which parts applied to me. STAGE.md settles the title and the file names, but not the rest.

question: What was the hardest thing to do?
answer: Scoping for a builder I cannot see. TASK.md demands a complete, polished game with no stubs, an action RPG has no natural end to its content, and I do not know how much budget or skill each builder will have. So I had to decide how much content is enough to show every mechanic, keep most of it as data, and write a cut order that removes whole features instead of leaving stubs. The next hardest was the network budget: a horde game in a shared world has to fit into 20 JSON messages a second, with unreliable ones under about 1,200 bytes.

question: What would you change in this prompt?
answer: Say what multiplayer 'on its own' should mean. Replace the WebGPU flags with the kit's list, or point at check.mjs. Tell the planner how much budget builders will have and whether they are all the same model, since that decides how big the plan should be. Say plainly that the planner may download the kit and run throwaway tests, and that scratch files should be removed afterwards, because only PLAN.md and this file are asked for. And mark which parts of TASK.md are for the builder only (exit interview, About screen, package name) and which the plan must cover.
